item.title: Govt approves Tk68.50 crore budget for workers' welfare in current fiscal
item.description:
The Ministry of Labour and Employment on Sunday approved a Tk68.50 crore budget for the Bangladesh Labour Welfare Foundation for FY27, alongside financial grants worth Tk12.98 crore for 2,199 workers and their families from both formal and informal sectors.
The decisions were taken at the 34th board meeting of the Foundation, held at the ministry's conference room on Sunday afternoon, with Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury presiding.
Speaking at the meeting, the minister said ensuring the welfare of the working class, standing by them in times of crisis, and strengthening the social safety net remain among the government's top priorities.
He said workers from both the formal and informal sectors continue to labour tirelessly, day and night, to keep the national economy moving and production systems running, adding that the country's development journey is being accelerated on the strength of their sweat and unrelenting effort.
The minister said the goal is to ensure that no working person feels alone in times of distress, noting that the ministry and the Foundation remain committed to protecting the rights and life security of workers at all times.
He expressed confidence that a balanced, work-friendly and exploitation-free labour policy and environment could be built through the coordinated efforts of government officials, employers and workers' organizations.
Labour and Employment Secretary Md Abdur Rahman Tarafder, Bangladesh Sramik Kalyan Foundation Director General Mohammad Kuddus Ali Sarker, Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal President Anwar Hossain, representatives from various ministries, and representatives from both workers' and employers' sides were present at the meeting.

item.description:
The number of student suicides in the country has risen steeply in the past 10 years and many families blame education system mismanagement as a contributing factor

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.

The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.

PM: Govt committed to building democratic, welfare-oriented state
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has said the government is working to build Bangladesh as a democratic and welfare-oriented state, with efforts underway to rebuild sectors devastated over the past one and a half decades.
“For more than a decade and a half, the fascist government destroyed the country’s education, healthcare, economy and other sectors. Now it is time to rebuild them,” he said. “We are continuing our efforts towards that goal. We believe the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will play an indispensable role in the country’s rebuilding journey.”
The prime minister made the remarks on Monday afternoon while inaugurating three SDG villages under the SDG Village Pilot Programme at the China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka.
Joining the event virtually, he formally inaugurated the three villages, Mitingachhari in Kaptai, Rangamati; Pankhali in Dacope, Khulna; and Nafanagar in Bochaganj, Dinajpur.
Tarique Rahman said no single ministry or department can achieve the SDG targets alone, stressing the need for cooperation from all relevant stakeholders.
He said the government’s people-oriented policies are aligned with the SDG principle of “leaving no one behind.” The government’s policy is “Bangladesh for All,” aimed at safeguarding the interests of people from all walks of life.
The prime minister said Bangladesh had demonstrated significant success in implementing the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and is similarly taking appropriate measures to effectively implement the SDGs.
Local Government Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury also attended the event.

item.title: Foreign minister: Govt yet to decide on PMs’ BRICS Summit attendance
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman on Monday said the government has not yet decided whether Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will attend the outreach session of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi next month, while urging the media to distinguish between two separate invitations extended by India.
“One is an invitation from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a bilateral visit, while the other is an invitation for the BIMSTEC chair to attend the BRICS Summit,” Khalilur told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
“First of all, I am not an astrologer. So, I cannot predict on which exact day it will happen,” he said when asked about the prime minister’s possible visit.
He also clarified that the invitation to attend the BRICS outreach session was not addressed to Tarique Rahman personally, but to Bangladesh in his capacity as chair of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC).
Khalilur was briefing reporters after Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.
On August 4, India confirmed that it had invited Tarique to attend the BRICS Summit as the current BIMSTEC chair, while a separate invitation for a bilateral visit to India has been in place since February.
“You would be aware that a formal invitation to Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit India was extended when he assumed office in February 2026,” Indian Ministry of External Affairs Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a recent media briefing in New Delhi.
“India has separately extended an invitation to the Bangladesh Prime Minister in his capacity as the current Chair of BIMSTEC to attend the outreach session of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi,” he said.
Jaiswal said the invitation was extended in line with the standard practice followed by BRICS for its outreach sessions, with other heads of regional groupings invited in a similar manner.
India will host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, with discussions expected to focus on global cooperation, trade and sustainable development.
During Monday’s meeting, High Commissioner Trivedi conveyed greetings from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and expressed India’s intention to work with the government and people of Bangladesh in a positive, constructive and forward-looking manner.
The two sides exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral relations through a people-centric approach.
Trivedi also paid a courtesy call on Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, with discussions focusing on bilateral relations and areas of common interest, including security cooperation.
The high commissioner conveyed India’s willingness to strengthen people-centric cooperation in all areas based on mutual interest, mutual benefit and mutual sensitivities.
BIMSTEC comprises seven countries — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
Bangladesh assumed the chairmanship of BIMSTEC in April 2025 for a two-year term, with a commitment to advancing regional cooperation and development.

item.title: Israel is going all out to stop Turkey from getting F-35s
item.description:
For the first time in years, Washington is discussing Turkey's return to the F-35 program as a serious possibility.

At the NATO summit in Ankara last month, President Donald Trump said he would lift the CAATSA sanctions that the U.S. imposed on Turkey after Ankara purchased Russian S-400 missile defense systems in 2019. Trump added that he was “certainly” considering restoring Turkey’s access to the F-35 program, which was also suspended at the time..

Notably, a separate sale of American engines for Turkey's domestic KAAN fighter jet has advanced through congressional review. Ankara is also reportedly exploring the transfer of its S-400 batteries to a Gulf state, a step Washington has demanded for years.

But the Russian system is no longer the only source of resistance. Israel argues that Turkish F-35s would, in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's words, "destroy the power balance" in the region. The phrase invokes Israel's “qualitative military edge,” a provision in U.S. law according to which Washington cannot sell weapons to Middle Eastern states if those arms would give them capabilities on par with Israel’s own weaponry.

Yet these rules have never been formally applied to Turkey, which is, after all, a U.S. treaty ally. What is being tested is thus not only an arms sale, but whether Israel's claim to regional primacy can restrict American policy toward a NATO ally.

How Turkey was pushed out


Turkey's search for a long-range air defence system predates the crisis by a decade. In 2009, the Obama administration approved a sale of Patriot missile defense munitions to Turkey, but the deal broke down over questions of price, technology transfer and local production. Ankara turned to a Chinese system in 2013, cancelled it in 2015, and signed with Moscow in 2017. A late American offer in 2018 came too late to reverse the Russian deal, and the first S-400 components arrived in July 2019.

But the S-400 decision was never simply the product of a failed arms negotiation. When Turkey downed a Russian jet in November 2015, it became the first NATO member to do so since the 1950s. As pressure from Moscow mounted, Ankara had to face it largely alone. The withdrawal of American and German Patriot batteries that same winter, even though armed groups in Syria still posed a threat, hardened Turkey’s sense of exposure.

The July 2016 coup attempt turned mistrust into a political rupture, particularly given that Fethullah Gülen, who Turkish authorities accused of orchestrating the coup, was living in the United States at the time.

Russia exploited the opening, filling Turkey's defense gap while widening the rift with its NATO allies. Turkish officials justified the purchase as an urgent requirement.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan gave it a second meaning. The real issue, he said, was not to the S-400 but to Turkey acting on its own will. Elsewhere he refused to retreat, saying Turkey was “not a slave.” Repeated at rallies, Erdogan’s rallying cry about the missile defense system turned it into an emblem of strategic autonomy, making the purchase as hard to reverse politically as militarily.

This has now become a political liability for Erdogan. In Turkey today, commentators and the main opposition describe the purchase as an act of stubbornness — one that left the S-400 rusting in a hangar and wasted the $1.5 billion Turkey had already paid for the F-35 program.

Turkey remains the only participant expelled after paying in, and the six aircraft it financed were never delivered. Its air force depends on an aging F-16 fleet, with Eurofighter Typhoons serving as a stopgap. The domestic KAAN fighter is the long-term answer, but its first batch is set to fly using American F110 engines under a $700 million sale that drew organized opposition in Congress before clearing review in July.

How Israel built a case against Turkey's return


Within 72 hours of the Ankara summit, Netanyahu took his objections to three American networks, arguing that Erdoğan was "not a friend" and could not be trusted.

The centerpiece of Israel’s case against Turkey was a remark by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. Asked on CNN Türk whether Turkey was among Israel's targets, the foreign minister said Israel had become a problem for the world and that, with these policies and this mindset, "these men have become a burden that humanity can no longer bear." The reference to "these policies" and "this mindset" pointed to the Netanyahu government, and the same judgment about Israel's isolation has surfaced in European capitals and at senior levels of the U.S. administration, from Trump to Vice President JD Vance.

But Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar recast the remark as dehumanizing Jews and calling for Israel's erasure, and this framing became the dominant account in Israeli commentary. Netanyahu carried it further on Fox, telling American viewers that Fidan had said the Jewish state must basically be wiped out.

The framing slotted Turkey into an existing category, the state that denies Israel's right to exist. But that is the language of Iranian state rhetoric, repeated by senior officials and inscribed on missiles. Turkey has never pursued such a policy; in fact, it supports a two-state solution and has recognized Israel diplomatically since 1949. Yet Israeli leaders, eager to drive a wedge into Ankara’s relationship with Washington, appear determined to cast Turkey as the next Iran.

Balance for whom?


The most revealing element of Netanyahu's argument was his definition of the regional balance. By telling Washington that Turkish F-35s would "destroy the power balance," he equated regional stability with continued Israeli superiority. Israel operates 48 F-35s and is contracted for 100, while Ankara's immediate effort centers on the six aircraft it already paid for. Turkey's return to the program would not erase Israel’s advantage; rather, it would modestly narrow an asymmetric order built around Israeli air power and freedom of action.

Israel’s concerns about Turkey are difficult to reconcile with Tel Aviv’s own increasingly preventive and attack-oriented doctrine. While Israeli officials like Netanyahu frame Turkish F-35s as evidence of "aggressive aspirations," Israeli aircraft have struck targets in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iran, Qatar, and Gaza. In Ankara, this is seen as hypocrisy; Netanyahu's "balance" is, in this reading, less about mutual restraint and more about preserving Israel's air superiority and freedom to strike.

Nor are the objections unique to Turkey. Since 2008, American law has required arms sales to Middle Eastern states be certified as preserving Israel's qualitative military edge, a standard Israel has invoked against countries including Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt. Nor is this only the position of Netanyahu. Naftali Bennett, his top rival in the coming election, told CNN that Israel cannot allow its Turkish “enemies” such advanced weaponry.

But applying the qualitative military edge doctrine to Turkey does not make sense for U.S. interests. Ankara is not a Middle Eastern buyer seeking parity with Israel but a NATO member whose air force anchors the alliance's southeastern defense, and its deterrent capacity is a European security question as much as a Middle Eastern one. Extending an Israeli veto over what Washington sells its own allies would put that doctrine in direct tension with NATO's requirements.

Israel's concern extends beyond the military effect of a stronger Turkish air force. Despite his best efforts, Netanyahu is unlikely to easily reverse Trump's broader opening to Ankara. By appointing his longtime associate Tom Barrack as ambassador there, Trump opened a new phase in Turkish-American relations. As Trump said when asked about Netanyahu’s opposition to giving F-35s to Turkey, "nobody tells me what we should be selling or not."

Unless Ankara takes a step that directly threatens Israel's security — an unlikely scenario — Trump has little incentive to abandon a relationship he finds useful. That relationship, more than the aircraft, is what Israel is working to prevent.

item.title: America, North Korea, and the Search for Peace
item.description:
The South Korean Buddhist monk, the Venerable Pomnyun Sunimin, in his book “What is Happiness?” introduces us to his philosophy of life: “Everyone born into this world has the right to be happy … and being helpful to the world and to others around us increases our own personal happiness.”

The U.S. is now ranked 24 out of the 147 countries surveyed by the Wellbeing Research Center at the University of Oxford in partnership with Gallup. Factors that contribute to this ranking include higher GDP per capita, a strong social support system, higher life expectancy, greater freedom, absence of government and corporate corruption and charitable giving. The U.S. ranking has dropped each year since 2011, with a significant decline between 2022 (ranked 15) and 2025 (ranked 24).

As a world leader, the U.S. is concerned with the world around us: With the wars in Ukraine, Iran, and Gaza and the innocent people killed; with the terrorism of October 7 and the innocent Israelis killed; armed conflicts in Sudan and Myanmar; insurgencies in Africa and Asia, and the criminal conflicts and the drug cartel violence in the Americas.

With this concern, there are understandable debates and doubts in the U.S. about a myriad of issues: the amount of aid we are providing to Ukraine, to defend itself from an invading Russia that’s receiving troops and weaponry from North Korea; efforts to peacefully negotiate a ceasefire with an Iran that says it has the right to enrich uranium and kill innocent peaceful protesters; an elusive peace in Gaza when Hamas refuses to disarm and tension in the West Bank intensifies; and a nuclear North Korea building more nuclear weapons and aligned with a revanchist Russian Federation. Helplessness with the conflicts in Sudan and Myanmar and the jihadist groups linked to Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State operating throughout Africa. Security concerns in Haiti and Ecuador due to gang violence and our inability to effectively counter the flow of illicit drugs coming into the U.S., primarily from Mexico, Columbia, and China. It’s hard to find happiness when assessing the world around us and the absence of peace.

Working with our allies and partners is an integral part of diplomacy and conflict resolution. NATO, AUKUS (Australia, the United Kingdom and the U.S.) and allies like South Korea, Japan and the Philippines are key to managing the ever-increasing security threats around the world. How we manage these relationships with our allies and partners is important.

Domestically, extreme political polarization has replaced polite political debate. A myriad of issues contribute to anxiety among the people: reported cuts to food stamps, Medicaid and social programs, with the rise in food and gas prices that receives daily media coverage. Nicolas Kristof of the New York Times reports a rise in homelessness in California, Oregon, and Hawaii and the plight of the Americans left behind. There’s extensive media coverage to rescind a planned $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and whether it was vandalism or shoddy construction of the Reflecting Pool in our Nation’s capital. Indeed, there are other political and social issues, like AI, that the average informed American is exposed to daily. Following these and other foreign and domestic issues is important for an informed electorate that will be voting in November and in 2028, but are we on overload? Of concern is the extreme polarization of views on these issues and the government’s responsibility to inform and seek the public’s support on these important issues, without adding to the polemics.

The author of “What is Happiness?” tells us: “Between 1995 and 1998, about three million people died of hunger and disease in North Korea and those who survived also suffered greatly as their family members, friends and neighbors died.” Despite North Korea’s formidable nuclear and missile capabilities, there are exigent health and food issues that continue to demand attention. The U.S. previously helped with these humanitarian issues because it was the correct thing to do. Returning to talks with North Korea to halt their nuclear and missile programs, with the lifting of sanctions and no longer demanding denuclearization as a condition for talks, would be the correct thing to do. It would be a positive development for Northeast Asia and the Korean people and hopefully contribute to the eventual reunification of the Korean Peninsula.

Progress with North Korea should bring some form of happiness to the Korean people and to the people in the U.S. who cry out for a more peaceful world.

FRANKFURT, Aug 10 (Reuters) - The German government regards U.S. President Donald Trump's latest Gaza plan as an opportunity to make progress towards the disarmament of Hamas, a German foreign ministry spokesperson said on Monday.

Asked in a regular news conference about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of the plan, the spokesperson also said some disagreement was to be expected.

"With such a complex undertaking, it was perfectly clear there would be many, many unanswered questions," he said.

item.title: Explainer-Trump's Gaza plan hinges on Hamas disarmament, Israeli withdrawals
item.description:
JERUSALEM, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Donald Trump's latest plan to end the Gaza war calls on Hamas to lay down its arms as Israel withdraws from the territory, terms endorsed by the militants but rejected by Israel, which says it will not pull back until the group's disarmament is complete.

WHAT IS TRUMP'S LATEST PLAN FOR GAZA?

The U.S. president on July 30 hailed what he described as a breakthrough in talks to advance a 2025 ceasefire plan, saying that Hamas and other Gaza militants had accepted a 15-point roadmap by his so-called "Board of Peace" to give up their weapons.

item.title: Where did the ivory trade go after China banned elephant tusks? North, into the Russian permafrost — where an estimated 10M frozen mammoths lie waiting, and a kilogram of tusk fetches up to $1,900.
item.description: Mammoth tusks came to be known as “ethical ivory” after China banned imports of elephant tusks in 2017, closing the market that elephants were being slaughtered to supply. China and Hong Kong are home to the world’s most developed tusk-carving industry, in which a single piece can sell for as much as billions of rubles (tens of millions of dollars). Meeting that demand fell to Yakutia‘s tusk hunters, who dig the frozen ivory out of the permafrost. The independent Siberian outlet People of Baikal describes how this punishing trade works — and what the hunters may be costing science and themselves. Meduza has translated the story in full.

item.title: Return of displaced Syrian Kurds to hometown suspended after violence
item.description:
The return of displaced Syrian Kurds to their northeastern hometown of Ras al-Ain was suspended on Monday after a first group of returnees was attacked, prompting protests in other Kurdish-majority parts of Syria.

Hundreds of people had gone back to the town on Monday, months after a January agreement with the Syrian government on merging Kurdish forces and civil institutions into the state that included provisions for the return of displaced Kurds.

item.title: Zelenskiy says he discussed defence, food security with Saudi crown prince
item.description:
KYIV, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he discussed a drone deal and food security with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Monday.

"There are domains in which Ukraine and Saudi Arabia can strengthen each other's ability to protect lives and people," he said on X after the call.

Speaking later in his nightly video address, Zelenskiy said a team of Ukrainian officials was in the region "and there are already areas in which our relations are developing well. I am counting on reciprocity in our mutual support."
